newsitem.title: USA: Shortages lift soyoil prices, gasoline gains again.
newsitem.headline: Shortages lift soyoil prices, gasoline gains again.

text.p: A surge in soybean oil exports coupled with already tight supplies sent prices for the oil sharply higher Thursday.
Gasoline prices rose again as a French refinery strike continued, while gold markets shook off rumours about big sales to end higher.

Exportable supplies of soybean oil, which is widely used in processed foods, have shrunk because the United States has shipped more than three times as much soyoil so far this season than at the same time last year.
"Things are pretty tight down there right now," one market source said. "I'm not sure the tightness will last, but they're having trouble loading right now."
A 45,000-metric-ton shipment to China temporarily drained supplies at U.S. export points, and had exporters aggressively hunting for supplies to fill a vessel scheduled for Dec. 12 departure.
"I don't think there's any volume for December (shipment) right now," said one exporter.

Robust exports this year came partly because of a small soybean crop in South America last year, leaving the United States as a key supplier until the next South America harvest in March, said Dan Cekander, analyst with FIMAT Futures.
The latest export data from the Department of Agriculture showed exports of 162,700 tons of soybean oil since the marketing year started on Oct. 1, up from 48,100 tons in the 1995 period.
Soyoil for December delivery rose 0.42 cent to 23.05 cents a pound at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Crude oil futures rose as bullish sentiment from tight supplies and a refinery workers' strike in Europe eclipsed the imminent addition of Iraqi oil on the market.
"The uptrend in crude continues as demand is good and supplies are tight," said Thomas Blakeslee, analyst with Cargill Investor Services.

The most recent oil inventory data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) showed crude oil stocks were 17.9 million barrels below a year ago when demand for crude in Asia was increasing, analysts noted.

Meanwhile, the strike by French oil workers at three refineries owned by French oil giant Elf Aquitaine entered its second week. The strike has crippled a quarter of French refinery capacity and may cut gasoline exports to the U.S.
"The strike has been big plus for gasoline all week, and thus a big plus for crude," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney, noting crude is needed to make gasoline.

Oil prices held up despite news Iraqi oil was being pumped into the Iraq-Turkey pipeline as a test under United Nations supervision. Turkey's Energy Ministry said it expects Iraqi oil to be pumped continually into the pipeline "within a week at the latest."

January crude oil rose 78 cents to $25.58 a barrel at the New York Mercantile Exchange. January heating oil ended up 1.54 cents at 75.11 cents a gallon and January gasoline added 1.44 cents to 69.68 cents a gallon.
Precious metals futures ended higher for the second straight session.

"If the rumours of the Bank of Portugal selling 25 (metric tons) to 30 tons of gold are correct, then the market has held up pretty well, suggesting it has now taken the brunt of producer and central bank selling in the past week or so," said Chris Foster, fund manager with Friedberg Mercantile Group.
February gold rose 50 cents to $373 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange.
